_comment: A.S.S. Score three-layer finding copy pools (src/threeLayer.js). Config-driven like roasts.json / fingerprints.json: edit copy here, NO code changes needed. One pool per breakdown key (filler, boilerplate, infoDensity, repetitive, crossPage, fingerprints, assets). Every finding gets an insight { roast, why, fix, evidence } where evidence is the finding string itself. Roasts carry ONE OR MORE {tokens} interpolated ONLY from that finding's real parsed evidence (token names documented per group below); a roast variant is only eligible when EVERY token it references exists in the finding's parsed tokens, and when the finding carries verbatim-evidence tokens (phrase/sentence/text/label/urls/host/alt...) the variant must cite at least one of them — variants whose tokens are missing are dropped (absolute rule: never fabricate details; a roast that can cite the real trigger must cite it). Token-free roasts are the fallback for findings with no interpolatable token at all. whys/fixes are business reasoning; they may carry OPTIONAL signal triggers — an entry may be an object { "text": "...", "triggers": ["tag", ...] }. A why/fix with triggers is eligible ONLY for findings whose evidence carries one of those tags (signalTagFor in src/threeLayer.js); a plain string (no triggers) is UNTAGGED and eligible for every finding of the group — it must stay genuinely signal-agnostic (no learn-more/cookie/legal/fact-check/stock/alt/filename/placeholder-style specifics; automated denylist test). When a finding has NO eligible why or fix line, that layer is omitted from the insight. Selection is deterministic: seeded by scan id + category + finding index via the same FNV-1a hashScanId the Slop Roast uses (same scan id -> identical insights, forever). Copy rules: loud/cheeky/meme tone, 1-2 sentences, pattern-based only — never assert AI authorship as fact (automated forbidden-phrase test). Token names per group: filler {count,words,density,phrase}; boilerplate {count,words,density,label,phrase,sentence,text,signalsNoun}; infoDensity {mattr,stopwordRatio,meanLen,sentences,shortPct,paragraphs,count,words,needed,examples,specificsNoun,factsNoun}; repetitive {kind,count,phrase,openings,sentences,paragraphs,repeatsNoun,appearancesNoun}; crossPage {pairCount,maxSim,urlA,urlB,sim,count,pages,pairsNoun}; filler additionally accepts {phrasesNoun,buzzwordsNoun} (plural-noun tokens filled from the finding count; no more "(s)" placeholders); fingerprints {scope,label,confidence} (count-token receipts — the “— N token usages (…)” suffix — additionally parse {count,topToken,topCount,tokenList} and carry the 'count-token' signal tag so gated whys/fixes apply only to them); assets {stockCount,fileCount,altCount,cleanCount,total,index,host,stem,alt,altKind,src}. CLEAN findings (zero/none measurements, healthy metric bands) render a compliment variant instead of a roast: { kind: 'clean', roast: compliment, why: cleanWhy, fix: keepUp, evidence } — pools compliments / cleanWhys / keepUps per category, same structural rules (1-2 sentences, <=220 chars, no AI-authorship claims, token-free by design; the evidence line carries the numbers). Negative findings keep roast/why/fix with no kind marker.

whys: Filler phrases signal that the copy was written to sound impressive, not to inform — and visitors who smell vague marketing lose trust in seconds.
The web is saturated with these exact same phrases. Every buzzword you reuse makes your site sound like everyone else's, not more credible.
Phrases like these add words without adding meaning — the page spends its word budget sounding important instead of saying what it does, and readers can't tell what you're offering.
Generic phrasing buries what you actually do: if the visitor can't tell from the first screen what the product is, they leave — and the site that says it plainly wins their attention.
When the copy sounds like a press release from 2014, the product behind it starts to feel just as dated — even if it isn't.
fixes: Delete each flagged phrase and replace it with plain English that names a real outcome — "elevate your brand" becomes "we redesign menus for restaurants."
Read the sentence out loud: if it would sound odd in a real conversation with a customer, rewrite it until it wouldn't.
Run a buzzword sweep with one rule: every claim must be backed by a fact, a number, or an example on the same page.
Before publishing, ask "would a competitor with the same template say this?" If yes, cut it or sharpen it.
Replace the filler with a specific differentiator: a number, a named feature, a customer outcome, or a deadline.
compliments: Zero buzzwords across the whole page. Somebody actually put the thesaurus down — and the copy reads better for it.
Not a single filler phrase in the entire scan. Your copy says things because they're true, not because they sound important.
We scanned the whole page for corporate wind and found none. The words here are actually doing their jobs.
No "game-changers," no "seamless experiences," no "unlock the potential." Just plain English doing real work.
Your page cleared the buzzword detector without even trying. The copy sounds like a human wrote it for humans.
cleanWhys: Copy without buzzwords reads as confident, and confidence is the entire game: visitors who understand you in one pass are far more likely to trust you and stay.
Plain, specific language is a differentiator now — while competitors stack synonyms, this page says something real, and that is what actually stands out.
Clear copy earns trust instantly because it costs the reader nothing to parse; the faster a visitor understands you, the sooner they believe you exist.
Jargon-free writing also ages well: it never sounds like a trend, so the page still reads as fresh in five years instead of like a time capsule.
Every sentence that says something beats ten that sound important — this page already knows that, and visitors can feel the difference.
keepUps: Keep writing the way you talk: specific, plain, and free of phrases that mean nothing.
Keep doing the buzzword sweep on new pages anyway — two minutes of hunting keeps the copy this clean.
Keep the thesaurus closed. Every plain sentence you publish is a differentiator while your competitors still sound like press releases.
Don't start decorating with "world-class" later. If it reads well today, it reads well tomorrow.
Keep holding every sentence to the standard that made this page clean: it must say something specific.

whys.text: Standard-issue lines like a copyright footer, a cookie notice or a "learn more" link are furniture, not content — every real site has them. They only start to hurt when legal text crowds out what you actually do.

whys: Every generic sentence is a wasted chance to say one specific thing about your product that a competitor cannot.

whys.text: When the compliance text outweighs the pitch, the visitor's takeaway is "this site is covering its ass," not "this site solves my problem."

fixes.text: Rewrite each flagged generic sentence with a concrete detail: swap "we are committed to quality" for "every order is checked by a human before it ships."
Keep legal and cookie text in one tight, honest block at the bottom — a copyright line in the footer is expected practice; the rest of the page is where your own voice should do the talking.
Replace "learn more" links with labels that say what the visitor will actually learn — "see pricing" or "read the case study."
Cut any line a competitor with the same website template could publish unchanged — that is exactly the kind of generic line to remove.
Do one pass where every sentence gets a fact check: if a sentence contains no verifiable claim, rewrite it until it does.

fixes: Make the flagged element earn its place: if it's required by law or contract, keep it — but keep it tight and out of the way; if it's filler, tighten it or cut it.

Every one of the {count} flagged {signalsNoun} in {words} words is legal-and-template furniture, not original writing. Your own voice lives somewhere else — let it.

compliments: Zero generic wording in the scan — no cookie-banner copy-pasta, no generic "learn more" wallpaper. The page reads written, not assembled.
No default-template sentences found. Every line on this page looks like it was typed for this business, not pasted from 40,000 others.
We looked for the usual suspects — cookie notices, legal text, newsletter blocks — and came back empty-handed.
Your copy is refreshingly free of standard-issue generic wording. This page says what it means instead of what templates mean.

cleanWhys: A page free of generic wording reads as written for the visitor rather than assembled from defaults — and that first impression is the whole credibility battle.
When nothing reads as filler, what you actually do becomes the only thing left to notice; every line earning its place gets the pitch full attention.
Original wording signals that the business behind the page is real — visitors have seen the template sentences so often that their absence is a genuine differentiator.
Readers have seen the same generic wording repeated across the web; pages that skip it come across as the original, not the echo.
Visitors scan for the usual template signs; when they aren't there, they spend that attention on your message instead of their skepticism.
keepUps: Keep the legal and cookie text in one quiet corner, and keep writing the rest of the page like this: specific and human.
Keep generic button labels off the page — if the visitor needs a button, name what it does.
Keep auditing for template sentences; the day one slips in, it will stand out more than it used to.
Keep your footer boring and your body interesting. That balance is exactly what this scan just rewarded.
Keep replacing "learn more" with real names for things — it's the habit that keeps generic wording out.

This page describes a business the way a fortune cookie describes your future: vaguely, and with confidence.
whys: Thin content gives visitors no reason to stay: if a page cannot answer "what do you do, and why you," the back button wins.
Thin content leaves the visitor with nothing to believe in — specific details (prices, dates, numbers, examples) are what make a product sound real.
Pages made of generic words around few facts read as substance-free next to a competitor who shows prices, dates and numbers.
Vague copy forces the reader to do your selling for you, and readers don't volunteer for that.
Every missing fact — a number, a date, a name — is a question the visitor now has to ask someone else. Usually your competitor.
fixes: Add at least one specific detail per paragraph: a price, a date, a number, a named customer, or a measurable result.
Turn short placeholder-ish paragraphs into real sections: state the claim, show the evidence, name the outcome.
Run a "would my competitor write this exact sentence" pass, and replace every yes with a specific detail about your product.
If a page can't reach roughly one specific detail per 75 words, write more substance before you write more sentences.
Cut hedging words and add proof: swap "we help teams scale" for "we helped 40 teams cut onboarding time by a week."
compliments: Strong word variety, few little filler words, and substantial paragraphs — this content is actually carrying information.
Your copy reads specific: dates, numbers, names, details — the things that make a visitor believe the business is real.
Solid numbers across the board: varied word choice, human-length sentences, paragraphs with actual substance.
This page is dense with real content — specific details per word well above the vague-copy line. The back button has no reason to fire.
The page is dense with useful content: every sentence earns its place instead of padding the word count.
cleanWhys: Specific details are what make a business credible: when the copy carries numbers, dates and named facts, the visitor stops wondering whether it's real and starts deciding whether it's for them.
Substantial content is the fastest way to look credible — pages that answer questions with real information read as the work of a real business, and this page already does.
Every specific detail removes a doubt the visitor would otherwise take to a competitor; the less vague the page, the fewer questions you leave unanswered.
Dense, varied copy respects the reader's time, which reads as respect for the reader — and that impression carries straight into how seriously the visitor takes the business.
A page that informs as it pitches does two jobs at once: it proves the product exists and gives the visitor the ammunition to justify choosing it with confidence.
keepUps: Keep the specific details coming: a number, a date, or a named customer per section is what kept this page off the vague list.
Keep writing paragraphs that hold at least one fact — it's the single habit that keeps content useful and skimming easy.
Keep the word variety up and the sentences human-length; both are free wins that pages like this one already banked.
When you expand the site, keep the same ratio — roughly one specific detail per 75 words — or this category stops complimenting you.
Keep trimming anything that adds words without adding information. The page is in the healthy band right now; stay there.

whys: Repeated sentences and paragraphs waste the reader's time and make the page feel assembled from leftovers rather than written for them.
Repetition dilutes your message — the line that matters gets exactly the same weight as the line that was just there, so nothing stands out.
Visitors skim; repeated phrasing makes the page feel longer and emptier, which reads as low effort and lowers trust.
Repeated text on one page splits the page's own signal, and repeated blocks across pages are exactly what repetition checks penalize.
Every repeat is a missed slot: that sentence could have said one new specific thing.
fixes: Keep each sentence's first three words distinct — it's the fastest fix for "everything starts the same."
Merge duplicated paragraphs into one, and use the freed space for a new point with a concrete example.
Draft once, then re-read with a highlighter: mark every sentence that restates an earlier sentence, and cut the second one.
After drafting, search the page for your top five phrases; if any appears more than twice, reword or delete the extras.
If a block genuinely must repeat (like a compliance line), move it to the footer once instead of restating it in the body.
compliments: No repeated sentence openings, no cloned paragraphs — every line on this page actually differs from the one before it.
Your sentences don't all start the same, and your paragraphs don't repeat. Boring to detect, delightful to read.
Structure check: clean. No stuck-record phrasing, no copy-paste paragraphs. The page varies like a real writer wrote it.
Zero duplicated openings and zero near-identical sentences — you used the paste button about as much as a novel should.
This page has genuine variety — the same amount of repetition as a well-edited article, which is to say almost none.
cleanWhys: Variety keeps attention: content that never repeats reads as shorter, sharper and more deliberate — the kind of page visitors actually finish.
Distinct sentences and paragraphs make the important lines stand out, so the message lands instead of blurring into a loop.
Fresh phrasing on every line reads as effort, and perceived effort is trust: pages that vary feel written for the reader, not recycled from a draft.
Variety also helps scanning — visitors who skim can find the new point in every block because no block is a repeat of the last.
A page that never repeats respects the reader's time, and nothing signals "we know you're busy" faster than not saying the same thing twice.
keepUps: Keep starting sentences differently — it's the cheapest way to stay out of the repetition report.
Keep paragraphs that say new things. If one ever says what another said, merge them and write a new point.
Keep varying the rhythm: short sentence, long sentence, and never the same opening twice in a row.
When you publish new pages, give each section a different opening line — that alone keeps this detector quiet.
Keep treating repeat phrasing as a draft symptom. The absence of it is exactly what this scan just noticed.

This site has the page variety of a buffet that only serves one dish.
whys: Near-duplicate pages split the effort you put into them: the work behind one version is repeated instead of extended, so the whole site reads thinner than it is.
Repeated content across pages makes the whole site feel like a shell — visitors who land on the same text twice assume there's nothing behind it.
Every page should earn its URL with a distinct purpose; pages that repeat just dilute the one message you actually need people to remember.
A real site is a set of answers to different questions; when all your pages answer the same question, visitors with any other question find nothing new.
Repeated content also burns trust — the faster a visitor can predict your next page, the faster they leave.
fixes: Give each page one job, and rewrite the main content so only that page says it.
Turn the repeated sections into unique value: add per-page specifics — prices, examples, testimonials from that vertical.
If two pages must be similar, merge them into one page and redirect the other.
Keep shared text (nav, footer, legal) out of the main content, where repetition checks look.
Before publishing a new page, diff it against your other pages; if the main content is 80%+ the same, start over.
compliments: No two pages are more than 80% the same — every page on this site actually earns its URL.
Cross-page check came back flawless: each page we compared has its own distinct main content.
Your pages aren't clones. We compared every pair and found nothing near-duplicate — rarer than it should be.
Every URL on this site answers a different question. The repetition detector packed up and went home.
Distinct content per page, confirmed across every pair — this is what a multi-page site is supposed to look like.
cleanWhys: Distinct pages mean the site answers more questions: every URL covers its own topic instead of repeating the same one, so the whole site feels bigger and more useful.
A visitor who lands on different, purposeful pages walks away thinking the business has depth — the exact flip side of a copy-paste site.
Unique content per page keeps every page worth its own visit — visitors find something new at each URL instead of the same page again.
Variety across pages makes the site feel bigger and more competent than any single-page clone ever can.
When each page earns its URL, the visitor's attention gets spent on new information every time — the best possible use of a visit.
keepUps: Keep giving each page one job; when a new page's main content starts resembling an existing one, that's the signal to rewrite.
Keep the shared stuff (nav, footer, legal) out of the main copy — that's exactly where repetition checks look.
Before publishing, diff the new page against the others; if it's 80%+ the same, the compliment disappears.
Keep letting each page carry its own specifics — prices, examples, answers — so no two pages ever need to say the same thing.
Keep growing the site page by page with unique content; the detector only complains when pages start doing each other's jobs.

whys: Recognizable template signs tell visitors the design is not yours — and if the design is borrowed, they start wondering what else might be.
A distinct look is a business asset; recognizable builder defaults make you blend into the 10,000 sites launched from the same kit this week.
The builder's defaults aren't tuned for your business — they're tuned for "looks fine" on any site, not for presenting your specific thing.
Design trust is earned in the first seconds; a generic look reads as low effort before the visitor has read a single word.
Even when the template is capable, unmodified defaults send the message that you shipped the draft.

whys.text: Component libraries are fine; shipping the stock vocabulary untouched is what marks the page as an unmodified starter. Visitors who recognize the default don't give you credit for the assembly.
A stock class list at this scale means the design system was inherited, not chosen — and what's inherited reads as disposable.

fixes: Replace at least the header, hero and button styles so the page doesn't carry the builder's default signature.
Customize the obvious giveaways first: colors, fonts, spacing, and any leftover placeholder assets.
Remove or replace the default tags and scripts that identify the builder — the "powered by" footers and CDN references.
Put one distinctive, real element on the homepage — an original illustration, a messy fact, a specific number — that no template ships.
If a builder feature is unused (stock icon packs, demo blocks), delete it; leftovers are what make the kit visible.

fixes.text: Replace the stock utilities on the elements visitors actually look at — hero, buttons, navigation — with your own color and typography tokens; keep the library, lose the off-the-shelf look.
If you're keeping the component library, define your own theme tokens and sweep the default class names out of the markup — the scan counts exactly those tokens, so removing them is the receipt.

compliments: No recognizable template signs — no leftover defaults, no off-the-shelf giveaways. This design looks genuinely yours.
We scanned the page for the usual builder signatures and found none. The template is not showing.

No leftover builder assets, no default icon packs — the page is wearing its own clothes, not the workshop's.

cleanWhys: A design with no template signs reads as owned and finished — visitors transfer that impression to the product or service behind it.
Original design is a differentiator that no amount of copy can fake; keeping the defaults buried keeps the site feeling built, not assembled.
When nothing on the page announces a kit, the visitor's mind goes to the work itself — and that's where you want it.
Unmarked builds also avoid the subconscious "10,000 sites launched from this template last week" reaction that erodes credibility.
A distinctive-looking site is remembered; the absence of the builder's signature is exactly the kind of detail that makes the difference.
keepUps: Keep customizing past the defaults — headers, styles, real assets — so the builder never shows its face again.
If you ever use a builder again, strip its markers before launch; that's the whole trick this scan looks for.
Keep the distinctive elements coming: original visuals and honest details are what push a site out of template territory.
Keep deleting unused demo blocks and default icon packs — leftovers are what make a kit visible.
Keep the hand-built touches; the absence of template signs is exactly what this category is here to notice.

whys.text: Stock imagery is instantly recognizable and instantly forgettable — it tells visitors nothing about your actual product, team, or customers.
Placeholder filenames and generic alt text are small clues that add up: together they read as "this site was never finished."
Alt text is accessibility: empty or generic alts lock out screen-reader users, who experience the page as "image, image, image" instead of a description.
Real photos of your product, team or workspace are the cheapest credibility upgrade a website can buy; stock photos cannot do that job.
Generic imagery makes your page interchangeable with every competitor who picked the same stock library's bestseller.

whys: The visual layer is judged in the first seconds — images that read as borrowed or unfinished quietly undermine everything else the page says, no matter how sound the copy is.

fixes.text: Replace stock and placeholder images with real ones: your product on a desk, your team in the office, your work in the wild.

Write real alt text for every image: what the picture shows and why it's on the page — not just a bare "image" label.
If an image is purely decorative, mark it as such instead of leaving empty or generic alt text.
Do a visual audit for the stock look (boardroom handshakes, fake smiles, floating laptops) and swap the top three offenders first.

fixes: Pick the single weakest visual this finding flagged and replace it with something only your business could produce — a photo of your real product, your real workspace, or your real people.
compliments: None of your images are stock or placeholder — your imagery actually looks like it belongs to this business. Refreshing.
Every image passed: real filenames, real alt text, no stock libraries. The visual side of this page is genuinely yours.
A completely clean image library — no "img3.jpg," no unsplash, no generic "image" alts. We didn't see that coming.
Zero generic-image signs, and every image carries real alt text. Screen readers thank you.
Your images look like your own: named descriptively, described properly, hosted on your turf. That's how it's done.
cleanWhys: Real, descriptive imagery builds credibility faster than any headline: visitors read "this is genuinely ours" before they read a single word.
Descriptive filenames and real alt text are free accessibility wins — every image works twice as hard when it's genuinely described.
Original visuals give visitors a concrete, memorable picture of who you are — exactly what stock photos can never provide.
Alt text that describes the image keeps screen-reader users in the conversation instead of narrating "image, image, image" at them.
An image library with no placeholder flags says the site was finished, not shipped — a small signal with outsized credibility value.
